newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine stockbrokers cry foul on new IPO system.
newsitem.headline: Philippine stockbrokers cry foul on new IPO system.

text.p: Philippine stockbrokers have criticised a new scheme for distributing initial public share offerings, saying it is a step backward from market reforms.

"Definitely we're not really for it. The broker is at the mercy of investment houses," Harry Liu, president of Summit Securities and a former governor of the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE), said on Wednesday.

Securities and Exchange Commission chairman Perfecto Yasay issued a memorandum on Monday requiring brokers to get their IPO allocations from underwriters. Previously brokers had obtained them from the PSE.

In the case of a "hot" issue, brokers cannot buy shares for their own account. In the case of a "cold" issue, brokers must not return unsold shares to the underwriter but must purchase them for their own account.
A hot issue is one that trades at a premium to its IPO on the grey market ahead a formal stock market listing. A cold issue is one that trades below its IPO price on the grey market.

Yasay said the new scheme was meant to ensure the wider distribution of IPOs. Some brokers have been accused of keeping IPO allocations for themselves under the old system instead of selling them to investors.
Brokers said the new scheme would remove the benefit of tapping the 177 operating members of the exchange as outlets for IPO allocation.
Under the old system, underwriters had to set aside 15 to 50 percent of an IPO for the PSE depending on the size of the issue. The PSE would then distribute the issue to its members.
Analysts said brokers that would suffer from the new ruling would be those with no affiliation to an underwriting or investment house.
"What's bad about this is that the capital of brokers would be at risk in the case of a cold issue," said Noel Reyes, research head of Anscor-Hagedorn Securities.
Brokers would now have to make a firm commitment to sell those shares, he added.
Under the old scheme, brokers could just return those shares if there was low demand for the IPO.
This would impact badly on small brokers, who constitute the main share of PSE membership, analysts said.
There are only about 20 major brokers on the PSE but they account for nearly 80 percent of trading volume.
